title: Chemistry IX · 2018 · E-Marking Notes (Questions & Solved Better Responses)
subject: Chemistry
introduction: This document has been produced for the teachers and candidates of Secondary School Certificate Part I (SSC-I) Chemistry. It contains official comments on candidates' responses to the May 2018 SSC-I Examination indicating the quality of the responses and highlighting their relative strengths and weaknesses.
generalObservations: In comparison to previous years, candidates attempted the paper well. However, there is still room for improvement. Key concepts on which teachers need to focus and give candidates more drill and practice include: (a) Balancing and construction of chemical equations and ionic equations, (b) Drawing of atomic structures for ions of elements, (c) Oxidation-reduction reactions occurring at the anode and the cathode in different electrolytic cells, (d) Process of crystallisation and effect of temperature on the solubility of different salts in water, and (e) Construction and working of a battery to produce electrical energy.

questions.questionText:
A student has incorrectly identified the branches of chemistry according to the descriptions given in his assignment.
Read the descriptions carefully and write the correct name of the branch of chemistry in the next column.
1. A subfield of chemistry dealing with radioactivity. It includes the study of the production and use of radioactive sources for a range of processes. (Incorrect: Physical Chemistry)
2. The study of chemical processes within and relating to living organisms. (Incorrect: Environmental Chemistry)
3. It deals with the qualitative and quantitative determination of chemical components of substances. (Incorrect: Organic Chemistry)
4. The branch of chemistry which applies physical and chemical processes for the transformation of raw materials into products on a large scale that are of benefit to humanity. (Incorrect: Nuclear Chemistry)
questions.sloText: Define chemistry and identify its major branches (physical, organic, inorganic, analytical, biochemistry, industrial, nuclear and environmental chemistry).
checkingHints: 1 mark each for identifying:
1. Nuclear Chemistry
2. Biochemistry
3. Analytical Chemistry
4. Industrial Chemistry
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses accurately matched all four descriptions to nuclear chemistry, biochemistry, analytical chemistry, and industrial chemistry. Weaker responses confused biochemistry with organic chemistry and industrial chemistry with physical chemistry, or merely rearranged the four incorrect branch names printed in the table.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses showed the correct identification of the branches of chemistry, i.e. nuclear chemistry, biochemistry, analytical chemistry and industrial chemistry for serial numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively. Candidates demonstrated clear understanding of each branch of chemistry with reference to its description provided in the question.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses demonstrated poor conceptual knowledge about the branches of chemistry. A few of these responses displayed correct identification of nuclear chemistry but failed to figure out the rest of the three branches. Mostly weaker responses couldn't determine the difference between the study carried out in the field of biochemistry and organic chemistry or physical and industrial chemistry. A few candidates played around with the incorrect responses given in the table and were unable to think beyond those names.
suggestions: Use real-world case studies to contrast overlapping branches (e.g., Organic Chemistry vs. Biochemistry, and Physical Chemistry vs. Industrial Chemistry).
Train students not to restrict their thinking only to words printed in a distractor column.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Nuclear Chemistry
2. Biochemistry
3. Analytical Chemistry
4. Industrial Chemistry

questions.questionText:
An atom of an element X has atomic number 12 and mass number 24. It loses 2 electrons from its outer most shell and acquires a +2 charge.
Draw the atomic structure of the ion of element X.
questions.sloText: Draw the atomic structure of the first twenty elements of the periodic table and their ions using their mass number.
checkingHints: 1 mark for nucleus with p = 12, n = 12.
1 mark for 2 concentric shells with 2 electrons in K shell and 8 electrons in L shell.
1 mark for square brackets with +2 charge outside.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses drew the magnesium cation [Mg]2+ with a central nucleus (p=12, n=12), two electron shells containing 2 and 8 electrons respectively, and square brackets with a +2 charge. Weaker responses drew the neutral magnesium atom (2, 8, 2) with 3 shells or omitted the brackets and +2 ionic charge.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses managed to draw the atomic structure of the given ion, i.e. magnesium ion. They illustrated the correct number of shells with exact number of electrons (2 in K, 8 in L) and charge of +2 on the ionic structure of magnesium.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses failed to draw the correct atomic structure for the given magnesium ion. A few of these responses displayed accurate structure for a neutral magnesium atom (with M shell still holding 2 electrons) but couldn't illustrate its ionic form. Some responses made careless errors such as omitting the charge, not drawing brackets, omitting the nucleus, or writing '2e-' and '8e-' as text rather than drawing electrons.
suggestions: Conduct side-by-side drawing drills of neutral atoms vs. cations/anions to highlight shell removal upon cation formation.
Enforce standard convention: central nucleus with p/n counts, electron dots on shells, and square brackets with superscript charge.
questions.modelAnswer:
Magnesium Ion [Mg]^(2+):
- Nucleus: p = 12, n = 24 - 12 = 12
- Electrons: 12 - 2 = 10 electrons (K = 2, L = 8)
- Diagram: Central nucleus [p=12, n=12] surrounded by 2 concentric rings (2 dots on inner ring, 8 dots on outer ring) enclosed in square brackets with +2 charge at top right.

questions.questionText:
a. Define electronegativity. (1 Mark)
b. Describe with reasons,
i. the change in electronegativity across the period in the periodic table. (2 Marks)
ii. the trend in shielding effect when going down a group of the periodic table. (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Define electronegativity and explain the periodic trends in electronegativity and shielding effect.
checkingHints: Part a (1 mark): Ability of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a molecule.
Part b.i (2 marks): Increases across a period (1 mark) due to smaller atomic size and higher effective nuclear charge (1 mark).
Part b.ii (2 marks): Increases down a group (1 mark) due to addition of new electron shells / inner electrons between nucleus and valence shell (1 mark).
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses defined electronegativity accurately with reference to a shared pair of electrons in a molecule, and clearly stated and justified both periodic trends. Weaker responses confused electronegativity with electron affinity ('ability to gain an electron') and stated trends without physical causes.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses accurately defined the term electronegativity as the ability of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a molecule. These responses included correct identification of the change in electronegativity across the period and trend in shielding effect down the group followed by logical reasons for their identification.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses showed poor understanding about the periodic trends of elements within a period and group. A few identified the trends correctly but couldn't justify their identification, or defined electronegativity as 'the ability to gain electron' (confusing it with electron affinity).
suggestions: Contrast the exact definitions of Electronegativity (attracting shared electron pair in a covalent bond), Electron Affinity (energy released when isolated atom gains an electron), and Ionisation Energy (energy required to remove an electron).
Require students to pair every periodic trend statement with its causal nuclear charge and shell-count explanation.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. The ability of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a molecule is called electronegativity.
b.i. Electronegativity increases across a period from left to right because atomic size decreases and effective nuclear charge increases, holding shared electrons more tightly.
b.ii. Shielding effect increases going down a group because new electron shells are added, placing more inner electrons between the nucleus and the valence shell.

questions.questionText:
There are two similar tea bags. One is placed in a cup of hot water while the other is placed in a cup of cold water.
i. In which cup will the water turn brown more quickly? (1 Mark)
ii. Explain your answer to part i with reference to the movement of particles. (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Explain the effect of temperature on the kinetic energy of particles and the rate of diffusion.
checkingHints: Part i (1 mark): Hot water cup.
Part ii (2 marks): Heating increases kinetic energy of liquid particles (1 mark), causing faster particle movement and rapid diffusion (1 mark).
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses identified the hot cup and linked thermal energy to increased kinetic energy, faster particle velocity, and rapid diffusion. Weaker responses identified the hot cup but misused scientific terms—writing 'electrons' instead of particles or 'effusion' instead of diffusion.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses comprehended the given information correctly and identified the hot cup as the one showing the change in colour of water quickly. Their reasons included concepts such as increase in kinetic energy, weakening of intermolecular forces, fast movement of particles, and increase in the rate of diffusion.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses exhibited lack of knowledge about diffusion in liquids and the effect of temperature on the rate of diffusion. Some identified the hot cup correctly but were unable to justify their identification, or wrote 'electrons' instead of particles and 'effusion' instead of diffusion.
suggestions: Demonstrate dye/tea diffusion in hot vs. cold water beakers and connect the macroscopic observation directly to Kinetic Molecular Theory.
Clarify terminology: molecules/particles vs. subatomic electrons, and diffusion vs. effusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Hot cup.
ii. When a liquid is heated, the average kinetic energy of its particles increases significantly. As a result, the particles move much faster and diffuse rapidly and easily throughout the water.

questions.questionText: A solution of copper (II) sulphate in water is saturated at 70°C. What will happen if the solution is cooled to 20°C? Give a suitable reason for your answer. (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Predict and explain the effect of cooling a hot saturated solution (crystallisation and solubility).
checkingHints: 1 mark for stating that crystals of copper(II) sulphate will form / settle at the bottom.
1 mark for explaining that solubility decreases as temperature drops from 70°C to 20°C.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses correctly stated that crystals of copper(II) sulphate form upon cooling because solubility decreases at 20°C compared to 70°C. Weaker responses confused cooling a saturated solution with freezing water or claimed the solution becomes unsaturated.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses interpreted the given information correctly and gave distinctive reasons for the formation of crystals at 20°C: less solubility at 20°C than at 70°C, reduced capacity to hold solute at 20°C, and excess solute separating out at the bottom in the form of crystals.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses failed to comprehend the information provided in the question. These responses presented the concepts of unsaturation and freezing rather than crystallisation and solubility with reference to temperature.
suggestions: Perform a practical crystallisation lab with copper(II) sulphate pentahydrate cooling from 70°C to room temperature.
Use solubility curves to visually demonstrate how cooling a saturated solution forces excess solute out as crystals.
questions.modelAnswer: When the saturated copper(II) sulphate solution is cooled from 70°C to 20°C, crystals of excess copper(II) sulphate will form and settle at the bottom. This occurs because the solubility of copper(II) sulphate decreases as temperature decreases, so the water can no longer hold all the dissolved solute.

questions.questionText:
During an experiment, MgBr2 and NaCl salts in their molten form are electrolysed in separate electrolytic cells.
Illustrate the reaction at anode and cathode in each electrolytic cell using balanced chemical equations.
a. MgBr2 (2 Marks)
   At the anode:
   At the cathode:
b. NaCl (2 Marks)
   At the anode:
   At the cathode:
questions.sloText: Write balanced half-equations for reactions at the anode and cathode during electrolysis of molten salts.
checkingHints: Part a (MgBr2): Anode: 2Br^- -> Br2 + 2e^- (1 mark); Cathode: Mg^(2+) + 2e^- -> Mg (1 mark).
Part b (NaCl): Anode: 2Cl^- -> Cl2 + 2e^- (1 mark); Cathode: 2Na^+ + 2e^- -> 2Na (1 mark).
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses wrote balanced half-equations showing oxidation of anions (Br- and Cl- to diatomic Br2 and Cl2) at the anode and reduction of cations (Mg2+ and Na+ to neutral metals) at the cathode. Weaker responses reversed the electrodes—oxidising neutral metals at the anode and reducing neutral halogens at the cathode.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses depicted in-depth understanding of oxidation-reduction reactions that occur during electrolysis of molten salts. Candidates used balanced chemical equations to present oxidation of bromide and chloride ions at the anode and reduction of magnesium and sodium ions at the cathode.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses exhibited poor conceptual knowledge and used irrelevant chemical equations. Majority of these responses showed oxidation of neutral magnesium and sodium atoms at the anode (Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e-) and reduced neutral bromine/chlorine atoms at the cathode (Br + 2e- -> Br-2), ignoring that molten salts already consist of ions.
suggestions: Emphasize that molten salts already contain free cations (Mg2+, Na+) and anions (Br-, Cl-) prior to electrolysis.
Use the mnemonic AN OX (Anode = Oxidation of anions to diatomic halogens) and RED CAT (Cathode = Reduction of cations to pure metals).
questions.modelAnswer:
a. MgBr2:
- At the anode: 2Br^- -> Br2 + 2e^-
- At the cathode: Mg^(2+) + 2e^- -> Mg

b. NaCl:
- At the anode: 2Cl^- -> Cl2 + 2e^-
- At the cathode: 2Na^+ + 2e^- -> 2Na

questions.questionText:
Give reasons why:
a. Mercury is used in thermometers. (1 Mark)
b. Silver is used in making jewellery. (1 Mark)
c. Copper is used to make water pipes. (1 Mark)
d. Reaction mixture of sodium and water turns red litmus paper to blue. (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Relate the physical and chemical properties of metals to their practical uses and chemical reactions.
checkingHints: Part a (1 mark): Liquid metal at room temperature, good conductor of heat, uniform thermal expansion.
Part b (1 mark): Shiny white lustrous noble metal, malleable, ductile, resistant to corrosion.
Part c (1 mark): Malleable/ductile, strong, does not react with water / corrosion resistant.
Part d (1 mark): Sodium reacts with water to form alkaline sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses linked each metal's specific physical or chemical property to its application and wrote the reaction of sodium with water forming alkaline NaOH. Weaker responses gave superficial answers or wrote misconceptions like 'copper is a bad conductor of electricity' or 'sodium explodes to turn litmus blue'.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses demonstrated logical reasoning skills. Candidates expressed the correct reason based on the properties of each metal: mercury's liquid state, heat conduction, and uniform thermal expansion; silver's shiny lustre, malleability, and ductility; copper's strength, malleability, and non-reactivity with water; and formation of alkaline NaOH when sodium reacts with water.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses were able to justify the use of any one metal only (mostly silver). Majority couldn't specify the uniform thermal expansion of mercury, or wrote false statements like 'copper is a bad conductor of electricity so no one gets shocked' or 'the exchange of electrons turns red litmus blue'.
suggestions: Connect specific engineering and household applications of metals to measurable physical properties (thermal expansion, malleability, corrosion resistance).
Demonstrate the sodium-water reaction with red and blue litmus paper to show alkali (NaOH) formation.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature, a good conductor of heat, and has uniform thermal expansion.
b. Silver is a shiny white lustrous metal that is malleable, ductile, and resistant to corrosion.
c. Copper is malleable, ductile, strong, and does not corrode or react with water.
d. Sodium reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide (2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2), an alkali that turns red litmus paper blue.

questions.questionText:
In 1911, a scientist proposed planetary model for an atom based on the given illustration of gold foil experiment.
i. Name the scientist who carried out the gold foil experiment. (1 Mark)
ii. Based on the given experiment, describe the FIVE main points of the planetary model of the atom as concluded by the scientist identified in part i. (5 Marks)
iii. Mention the TWO fundamental defects in the planetary model of the atom. (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe Rutherford's gold foil experiment, the postulates of his planetary atomic model, and its fundamental defects.
checkingHints: Part i (1 mark): Ernest Rutherford.
Part ii (5 marks): 5 conclusions from Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment.
Part iii (2 marks): 2 fundamental defects (electron spiraling into nucleus; continuous spectrum vs. observed line spectrum).
questions.overallPerformance: Question 7a was attempted by the vast majority of candidates. Better responses named Rutherford, listed five distinct conclusions linking experimental observations to atomic structure, and stated both classical radiation defects. Weaker responses confused Rutherford with Bohr or Thomson, or listed experimental setup details instead of model conclusions and defects.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses identified Rutherford as the scientist who performed the gold metal foil experiment, specified five clear postulates concluded from the experiment (empty space, positive nucleus, small dense core, revolving electrons, electrical neutrality), and accurately stated the two fundamental defects regarding continuous energy emission and line vs. continuous spectra.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses identified the name of the scientist and mentioned one or two common conclusions, but couldn't figure out the defects present in Rutherford's atomic model. A few identified the scientist as Bohr or J.J. Thomson and wrote irrelevant postulates.
suggestions: Teach Rutherford's experiment using a three-column table: Observation -> Deduction/Postulate -> Classical Defect.
Contrast Rutherford's continuous spectrum prediction with Bohr's quantised line spectrum resolution.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Ernest Rutherford.
ii. Five Main Points:
1. Electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular orbits.
2. Most α-particles passed undeflected, proving most of the volume of an atom is empty.
3. Deflection of a few particles showed there is a central positive charge called the nucleus.
4. Complete rebound of a few particles showed the nucleus is hard and dense.
5. All fundamental particles except electrons lie within the nucleus (nucleons), and proton count equals electron count.
iii. Two Defects:
1. According to classical electromagnetic theory, a revolving charged electron should emit energy continuously and spiral into the nucleus.
2. Continuous energy emission should produce a continuous spectrum, whereas a line spectrum is experimentally observed.

questions.questionText:
i. Name and describe the types of bonds and their formation in the following species. (7 Marks)
   I. A water molecule (H2O)
   II. A hydronium ion (H3O^+)
ii. Mention ONE similarity between the bonds identified in part i. (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Describe covalent and coordinate covalent bonding in water (H2O) and hydronium ion (H3O+).
checkingHints: Part i.I (3.5 marks): Covalent bond in H2O; mutual sharing of electrons between O and two H atoms; Lewis dot-and-cross structure.
Part i.II (3.5 marks): Coordinate covalent (dative) bond in H3O^+; donation of oxygen lone pair in H2O (donor) to empty shell of H^+ proton (acceptor); diagram with arrow.
Part ii (1 mark): Both bonds are formed by sharing a pair of electrons.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses clearly distinguished mutual electron sharing (covalent bond in H2O) from lone-pair donation to an electron-deficient proton (coordinate covalent bond in H3O^+), supported by Lewis structures with dative arrows, and noted that both bonds share electron pairs. Weaker responses invented non-existent bond names ('ionization bond', 'chemical bond') or drew H3O^+ without a coordinate arrow.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses identified the type of bonding present in H2O (covalent bond) and H3O^+ (coordinate covalent bond), described the formation of bonds in each species in detail (identifying donor H2O and acceptor H^+), supported their description using dot-and-cross diagrams with arrows, and stated that both bonds are formed by sharing of electrons.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses gave incorrect definitions of all types of chemical bonds. Some drew the dot-and-cross structure of water but called it an ionic bond, or drew H3O^+ with three single covalent bonds without showing the dative arrow or +1 charge, and failed to state the similarity.
suggestions: Emphasize how H2O transitions into H3O^+ by donating one of oxygen's two lone pairs to a proton (H^+).
Insist on drawing the coordinate arrow (donor -> acceptor) and brackets with +1 charge for polyatomic cations.
questions.currentTopic: Structure of Molecules & Coordinate Covalent Bonding
questions.modelAnswer:
i.I. Water (H2O): Contains single covalent bonds formed by mutual sharing of electrons where each H atom shares 1 electron with O.
i.II. Hydronium ion (H3O^+): Contains a coordinate covalent (dative) bond where oxygen in H2O (donor) donates a lone pair of electrons to an empty shell of H^+ ion (acceptor): H2O + H^+ -> H3O^+.
ii. Similarity: Both covalent and coordinate covalent bonds are formed by the sharing of an electron pair between two atoms.

questions.questionText:
i. Describe the density of solids and gases based on the strength of intermolecular forces present among their particles. (4 Marks)
ii. Differentiate between amorphous and crystalline solids on the basis of the following properties. (3 Marks)
• Geometrical shape
• Melting points
• Symmetry
questions.sloText: Explain the density of solids and gases based on intermolecular forces and differentiate between amorphous and crystalline solids.
checkingHints: Part i (4 marks): Solids have very strong intermolecular forces and closely packed particles -> high density (2 marks); Gases have very weak intermolecular forces and large empty spaces -> very low density (2 marks).
Part ii (3 marks): 1 mark each for contrasting geometrical shape, melting points, and symmetry.
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses linked strong intermolecular forces and tight packing in solids to high density, contrasted that with weak forces and large spaces in gases causing low density, and tabulated accurate distinctions for amorphous vs. crystalline solids. Weaker responses claimed gases are denser than solids or confused symmetry with allotropy/anisotropy.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses described the density of solids and gases based on the difference in intermolecular forces and inter-particle spacing, and provided a clear comparative table distinguishing amorphous and crystalline solids across geometrical shape, melting points, and symmetry.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses demonstrated lack of knowledge regarding the properties of gases and solids. Some claimed gases are denser than solids, or understood geometrical shape but wrote wrong descriptions for melting point and symmetry (confusing symmetry with allotropes or specific crystal shapes like hexagonal vs. tetrahedral).
suggestions: Reinforce the causal chain: Strength of Intermolecular Forces -> Inter-particle Spacing -> Mass per Unit Volume (Density).
Use structured comparison tables for crystalline vs. amorphous solids covering shape, melting point, cleavage, and symmetry.
questions.currentTopic: States of Matter & Types of Solids
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Gases have very low density because intermolecular forces are very weak and molecules are far apart with large empty spaces. Solids have the highest density because intermolecular forces are very strong, packing particles tightly together in fixed positions.
ii. Amorphous vs. Crystalline Solids:
1. Geometrical shape: Amorphous solids are shapeless/irregular; Crystalline solids have a definite 3D geometrical shape.
2. Melting points: Amorphous solids do not have sharp/fixed melting points; Crystalline solids have sharp and fixed melting points.
3. Symmetry: Amorphous solids are non-symmetric; Crystalline solids are symmetric.

questions.questionText:
Given below is zinc-carbon battery.
i. What is the anode, cathode and electrolyte made up of in the given dry cell battery? (3 Marks)
ii. How does the zinc-carbon battery work? Support your answer using balanced chemical equation for the reactions occurring at the anode and the cathode. (4 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe the construction and electrochemical working of a dry cell (zinc-carbon battery).
checkingHints: Part i (3 marks): Anode = Zinc (1 mark); Cathode = Carbon/graphite rod (1 mark); Electrolyte = moist paste of NH4Cl and MnO2 / ZnCl2 (1 mark).

Part ii (4 marks): Explanation of electron flow from Zn anode to graphite cathode (2 marks); Anode equation Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e- (1 mark); Cathode equation 2NH4+ + 2MnO2 + 2e- -> Mn2O3 + 2NH3 + H2O (1 mark).
questions.overallPerformance: Better responses accurately named the graphite cathode, zinc anode, and NH4Cl/MnO2 electrolyte paste, explained the external flow of electrons from zinc oxidation to cathode reduction, and wrote balanced half-equations. Weaker responses merely labeled anode and cathode as 'negative and positive terminals' and wrote illogical equations like 'C + 2e- -> C'.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses demonstrated correct identification of anode (zinc), cathode (graphite), and electrolyte (powder/paste of NH4Cl and MnO2). Candidates explained the stepwise loss and gain of electrons at the anode and cathode respectively and supported their explanation with balanced chemical equations.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses exhibited poor knowledge regarding the working of a dry cell. Candidates struggled to identify the materials of the anode, cathode, and electrolyte (merely calling them '-' and '+' terminals) and wrote illogical half-reactions such as 'C + 2e- -> C' at the anode and 'Zn -> Zn+ + 2e-' at the cathode.
suggestions: Use a cross-sectional diagram of a Leclanché dry cell to teach the chemical identity and role of each component.
Practice writing half-cell equations for common commercial batteries (dry cell, lead-acid accumulator, alkaline cell).
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Cathode is made of graphite (carbon rod), anode is made of zinc metal container, and electrolyte is a moist paste of NH4Cl and MnO2 (with ZnCl2).
ii. When the terminals are connected through a wire, zinc (having high oxidation potential) loses electrons (oxidation): Zn -> Zn^(2+) + 2e^-. These two electrons travel through the wire to the graphite cathode where the electrolyte undergoes reduction: 2NH4^+ + 2MnO2 + 2e^- -> Mn2O3 + 2NH3 + H2O, converting chemical energy into electrical energy.
